analysis.one_liner: Requires lenders to hold a mediation with homeowners, plus a counselor, before any foreclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a June 2010 subcommittee hearing and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011, without a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any lender foreclosing on a federally insured, guaranteed, or Fannie/Freddie-eligible mortgage on a one- to four-family home to first sit down with the borrower and a certified housing counselor for a one-time mediation, paid for by the lender. It applied to the mortgagee of record, including MERS acting as a nominee. It was introduced by Rep. Marcia Fudge in February 2010 and never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure on federally backed mortgages, who would get a guaranteed chance to meet their lender face-to-face with an independent counselor present before losing their home — at the lender's expense rather than their own.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners facing foreclosure on federally backed loans

how_it_helps.text: Before initiating a foreclosure or sheriff sale, the mortgagee would have to conduct a one-time mediation with the borrower and a HUD-certified housing counseling agency, at the mortgagee's own expense [S3].
The requirement would cover loans insured or guaranteed by federal housing programs, including FHA, VA, rural housing, and loans eligible for purchase by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac [S3].

The bill would apply to any entity acting as mortgagee of record for a lender, including MERS, closing a route by which foreclosure filings were made by parties with no direct relationship to the loan [S3].
The mediation would be available only in ways consistent with applicable state and local requirements, and a homeowner could bring a certified counselor at no personal cost [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and loan servicers, who would bear the cost of the mediation and the delay before they could complete a foreclosure on a federally backed home loan.

drawbacks.text: Mediation is not a loan modification: the bill would require a meeting, not a new deal, so a homeowner could go through mediation and still lose the home [S3].
Mandatory mediation adds a procedural step and delay to every covered foreclosure, and lenders could pass those costs on to other borrowers through fees or pricing [S3].
The requirement would cover only mortgages with a federal connection — insured, guaranteed, or Fannie/Freddie-eligible — leaving purely private-label mortgages outside it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For homeowners in foreclosure, a guaranteed sit-down with the lender and a free counselor is a real safeguard at a moment when mistakes and lost paperwork routinely cost people their homes. The honest costs are added delay and expense in foreclosures that might have gone faster, and the bill does not force lenders to actually offer relief — it forces a conversation. On balance the help to at-risk homeowners outweighs the procedural burden on lenders, but the bill is narrow and does not guarantee outcomes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, got a subcommittee hearing in June 2010, and then sat with no committee vote or floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcia Fudge introduced the bill on February 22, 2010, with original cosponsors including Maxine Waters, Kendrick Meek, Betty Sutton, and Mary Jo Kilroy [S3].

It was referred to the Financial Services Committee and, for portions in its jurisdiction, the Veterans' Affairs Committee; the Veterans' Affairs portion went to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity [S5].
A subcommittee hearing was held on June 10, 2010, but neither committee ever approved the bill and it never reached the House floor [S5].
Ten House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans did [S4].
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers are better off because the bill died: they never had to fund a pre-foreclosure mediation with a borrower and counselor. Homeowners facing foreclosure got no new federal right to sit down with their lender before losing their home.

for.name: Marcia Fudge
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and lined up 10 Democratic cosponsors

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Held primary jurisdiction over housing finance
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill after a June 10, 2010 subcommittee hearing, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republicans signed on, and the bill died in a Democratically controlled House without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to pay for a mandatory mediation with each borrower and counselor before foreclosing on a federally backed loan, adding cost and delay to the foreclosure process. Their interest in completing foreclosures quickly ran against the homeowner's interest in a mediated review.

The bill would have made certified housing counselors a required participant in every covered pre-foreclosure mediation, at the lender's expense, giving agencies a guaranteed new role in the foreclosure process.

The bill would have expressly covered entities like MERS acting as mortgagee of record for a lender, so foreclosure filings could no longer be brought only by a nominee with no counselor-mediated review. MERS exists to streamline foreclosure filings, an interest that runs against homeowners facing foreclosure.
